paragraphs.heading: Updating a belief
paragraphs.text: Bayesian inference is a way of doing statistics that uses Bayes' theorem to put a probability on a hypothesis and then revise it as new information comes in. At its heart, it starts from a prior distribution, what you believed before, and uses it to estimate posterior probabilities, what you believe after. It is an important technique in statistics, above all in mathematical statistics.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is used
paragraphs.text: This kind of updating is especially important when a sequence of data is analysed as it unfolds. It has been used in science, engineering, philosophy, medicine, sport, psychology and law. In decision theory it is closely tied to subjective probability, which is often called Bayesian probability.

paragraphs.heading: Hypothesis and evidence
paragraphs.text: H stands for a hypothesis, any claim whose probability the data might change, and E stands for the evidence, the new data. Often several hypotheses compete, and the job is to find which one is most probable. P(H), the prior probability, is your estimate for H before you see E. P(H∣E), the posterior probability, is the chance of H once E has been seen, and that is the number you are after.

paragraphs.heading: Likelihood and model evidence
paragraphs.text: P(E∣H) is the likelihood: the chance of seeing E if H is true. With H held fixed, it shows how well the evidence fits that hypothesis. P(E), sometimes called the marginal likelihood or model evidence, must be above zero, or Bayes' theorem would divide by zero. It is the same for every hypothesis being weighed, so it does not change which hypothesis comes out ahead.

paragraphs.heading: What decides the answer
paragraphs.text: When comparing hypotheses, only two things move the posterior: the prior and the likelihood. A hypothesis ends up more probable in proportion to how plausible it was to begin with. It also gains in proportion to how well it fits the new evidence.

paragraphs.heading: Again and again
paragraphs.text: After more evidence arrives, the same steps can simply be run again. When many possible models are in play, each one gets a degree of belief. If the models are described by parameters, the belief in all of them can be updated at once. Belief over the models then becomes belief over the values of the parameters.

paragraphs.heading: Is it the only sensible rule
paragraphs.text: Bayesian updating is widely used and easy to compute with. Even so, it is not the only rule for updating that might count as rational. Ian Hacking pointed out that the classic "Dutch book" arguments do not force Bayesian updating, and other rules that also avoid Dutch books exist. Such rules have been discussed since Richard C. Jeffrey published his rule, which applies Bayes' rule when the evidence itself is given a probability.
